findings.source_grounded_note: Vergennes’s strategic revenge brings war, restored prestige, and enormous debt. Turgot warns that intervention will defeat financial reform; distinguish contemporary perceived victory from the source’s judgment that lasting British weakening was not achieved.

Economies and confidence are meant to balance ordinary finance while loans meet extraordinary costs. High interest and generous terms qualify Necker’s personal-credit explanation; no new direct tax during his tenure does not mean the war was paid for.

findings.topic: Compte rendu and enduring fiscal expectations
findings.source_grounded_note: The 1781 published ordinary surplus omits war’s extraordinary accounts from public scrutiny. Its prestige underlies Necker’s resignation dispute and later comparisons that discredit successors. Joly de Fleury raises taxes and further loans.

Court connections and useful splendour support borrowing before slowing subscriptions and expiring taxes expose debt-service, redemption, and anticipation pressures. His lavish image coexists with a radical reform plan.

An exemption-free land tax in kind would replace vingtièmes, with taxpayer assemblies cooperating with intendants; stamp duty and domain reforms supplement it. Preserve proposed design from subsequent modification.

Grain freedom, internal customs abolition, corvée commutation, and Anglo-French trade treaty aim at productive recovery; delayed yields require interim loans, hence the search for national endorsement.

Calonne rejects unpredictable elected Estates-General for nominated notables, expecting status/gratitude to bring compliance. Composition, administrative experience, delay, and Vergennes’s death undermine this calculation.

They accept equality of taxation and representative assessment in principle, but contest indefinite variable land burdens, collection in kind, seat guarantees, intendant veto, and clerical debt redemption. Hostility to Calonne must not be equated with blanket rejection of reform.

findings.topic: Necker’s reputation, accounts, and authority to consent
findings.source_grounded_note: Comparison with 1781 makes deficit claims suspect. Demands for accounts and doubt about whom nominees represent lead to the claim that only Estates-General can approve new taxes.

Leaks and pamphleteering precede Calonne’s attempt to mobilize unprivileged opinion against notables. The appeal fails; dismissal discredits the minister and reinforces the opposition rather than producing the intended social division.

Lamoignon takes judicial office; Necker’s unauthorized defence brings exile; royal reluctance yields to Brienne as falling stocks threaten credit. Modified cash/time-limited taxation and corporate representation initially seem negotiable.

findings.topic: Royal veto of audit and collapse of the Notables strategy
findings.source_grounded_note: Confused accounts produce demand for permanent auditors; the king treats oversight as a threat to prerogative. Lafayette calls for national representation; dissolution leaves reform formally alive but deprives it of legitimating endorsement.

Support for Dutch patriots collides with British/Prussian backing for Orange. Financial weakness prevents preparation and intervention as Prussia occupies the Republic, linking domestic crisis to diplomatic humiliation.

Grain/corvée reforms pass relatively easily, but stamp tax and territorial subvention meet account/consent demands. Forced registration prompts illegality declarations, Calonne proceedings, and exile to Troyes; Bordeaux’s provincial-assembly objections form a distinct dispute.
Crowds, salons, clubs, pamphlets, and displaced law clerks support magistrates. Closure of clubs, print restrictions, troops, and exile restore apparent order without restoring political confidence.

Withdrawal of new taxes in exchange for prolonging vingtièmes ends exile; economies, accounts, loans, and eventual Estates-General promise recovery by 1792. The compromise disappoints provincial courts and public supporters.

findings.topic: Royal Session and assertion of will
findings.source_grounded_note: A session meant to permit free opinions likely has support for loans, but royal ordering of registration and the reply to Orléans convert potential success into a despotism controversy. Distinguish Royal Session from an announced lit de justice.

Civil-rights legislation accompanies financial business as conciliation, yet registration is delayed amid conflict over exiles and lettres de cachet. Link legal emancipation to its political context without reducing it to financial policy.

Nominated assemblies compound vingtièmes or suffer punitive assessments; this strengthens arguments for stronger provincial estates. Nomination, fiscal bargaining, and representative power remain distinct dimensions.

findings.topic: Fundamental laws and arrest of magistrates
findings.source_grounded_note: Paris asserts inheritance, property, customary/provincial rights, irremovable magistracy, Estates-General consent, registration, and freedom from arbitrary arrest. D’Eprémesnil and Goislard’s refuge/arrest dramatize the standoff.

findings.topic: Lamoignon’s judicial coup and reform publicity
findings.source_grounded_note: Plenary Court transfers registration powers, grands bailliages cut parliamentary jurisdictions, offices disappear, and criminal-law reform seeks enlightened support. Formal reform benefits cannot be detached from the bid to maintain absolutism.

findings.topic: Nationwide resistance and limits of the noble-revolt label
findings.source_grounded_note: Lawyers, lower courts, clergy, nobles, and urban crowds resist; Grenoble’s Day of Tiles, Rennes, and Pau illustrate different dynamics. Officers hesitate but no officer is said to disobey decisive orders; judicial paralysis is widespread but uneven.

findings.topic: Invitation to debate Estates-General and failed division
findings.source_grounded_note: July’s consultation seeks distraction, division, and reassurance, yet public attention continues to attack the ministry until it falls. Later political effects must not be projected prematurely onto July.

Tax arrears and policy chaos undermine anticipations; July hail reduces expected tax yields, and financiers threatened by centralization decline support. Announcing Estates-General fails to restore credit; suspension of payments, forced paper, panic, and Necker’s recall follow.
Brienne’s and Lamoignon’s projects disappear and Necker accepts a caretaker role. The chapter concludes that collapse is political and intellectual as well as financial, leaving a power vacuum.
